title: Something in the ending of Perfect Blue

commenti.body:
The way I see it, after Mima spends some time coming to believe that she herself might be a killer, this is her reasserting that she isn't anything like that at all. It stands as a refutation of a culture that too often has people casually wishing death upon people that they don't like. 

And there's the added layer of Rumi not really being Rumi at that point the narrative: she's Mima, and it could be said that Mima is actually saving herself. Beyond the split personality thing, Rumi is indeed a version of what Mima could turn out to be: a former idol whose career didn't take off, and is driven to mental distress by her experiences in the industry.

I actually love all of this. I think the first idea works so well, especially because Mima's act of compassion comes directly after she declares that she knows who she is to rumi. In saving the "idol Mima" she's rejecting the idea that she should be anything like her.

Like the "idol Mima"/Rumi being obsessed with the destruction of the other Mima as well as being violent af. Mima rejects both of those things through her act of compassion, thus saving the "idol Mima" is what allows Mima to essentially kill her (as in the hallucination dopple-ganger). 

Also yes, I also love love the idea that this is Mima saving herself, as in her future. That's also so genius

Solidarity I guess. Mima and Rumi understand exactly what the other is going through and both are kind people who want to help each other. Perhaps, the past and future versions of a same person helping each other.

/u/phildy already wrote a good reply so I just want to bring up a new point:

Mima probably feels that Rumi is a victim of idol culture too. That does of course not excuse her actions, but it does explain while Mima feels sorry for her.

Japan (and South Korea too I guess) is pretty unique when it comes to idol culture. It's a really weird phenomenon that makes no sense in other advanced modern democracies. These idols are put on a pedestal and are not allowed to live a normal life. They can't even date. Who decided this? Their managers of course. 

People like Rumi are insane and must take responsibility for their actions, but I can almost guarantee you that their lives would have looked very different outside of Japan. There is of course a chance that something other than idols would have made her lose her mind, but we don't know that for sure.

Also, the fact that the headlights are seen as stage lights by rumi. Mima physically knocks Idol Mima/rumi away from the stage lights. In doing so she's now fully retiring her idol self, for both her and Rumi?
